transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, so, I guess what finally pushed me to come in is... well, I'm a software developer, and my job involves a lot of sitting, and lately I just... I keep getting up when I really, really shouldn't. 

Like, we have these long sprint planning meetings for work—if you know anything about software development, you know how tedious those can be, but they are important to the team—and I just can't seem to stay in my chair. Even when I know I absolutely need to stay put and be on camera. And it's not just work, either. The other day, I was on a really important call with my mortgage broker, just sitting there going over the interest rates and escrow and all that heavy stuff, and right in the middle of it I just stood up and walked away because I suddenly felt like I desperately needed a glass of water right that exact second. 

Or I'll just randomly decide I need to go check something in the other room, like if I left a coffee cup on the counter, right in the middle of someone talking. I know I should just sit there—I mean, I'm 40 years old, I should be able to just sit through a meeting or a phone call without wandering off—but my brain just sort of says 'go do this now' and I'm out of my chair before I even really think about how bad it looks. It's not completely ruining my life or anything, but it's just getting so incredibly frustrating to deal with every day.
Do you often have trouble sustaining your attention when you’re reading, working, or listening to someone speak?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It's actually a huge part of why things take me so much longer than they probably should. Like, okay, for example, at work I have to review pull requests—that's when another developer writes code and I have to read through it to make sure it's solid before we merge it into the main project. And I always, always sit down to do it with the absolute best intentions. I'll close my other tabs, I'll tell myself, 'Okay, you are going to focus and get this done right now.' 

But then, maybe just a few minutes in, I'll suddenly realize that I've been staring at the exact same block of code, or the exact same line, for I don't even know how long. Because my eyes are technically looking at the screen, but my brain is suddenly thinking about five completely unrelated things. I'll be wondering what I'm going to make for dinner, or if I remembered to reply to an email from three days ago, or why they decided to cast a certain actor in that movie I watched last night, or if I need to buy more dog food. 

And it was the exact same thing with those mortgage documents I was talking about earlier! I tried to read through the escrow terms by myself before that call—and I really, really wanted to understand them because, you know, buying a house is a massive financial commitment and you absolutely do not want to mess that up or miss some hidden fee. But I just kept finding myself reading the exact same paragraph over and over and over again. I'd start with good intentions, read a sentence, and then realize I was just looking at the paper while my mind was completely somewhere else. It's like the words just stop registering after the first couple of minutes, no matter how hard I try to force myself to care about what I'm reading. It's exhausting, honestly, having to reread everything four times just to get the basic gist of it.
Did you have these kinds of attention problems when you were a child?

Oh, wow, childhood. Um... yes, actually. I mean, it's funny you ask that because I was just talking to my mom about this the other day. She was helping me pack some boxes for the move, and we found this old folder of my report cards from elementary school. And it was just... it was wild reading through those teacher comments, because it was exactly the same stuff I'm dealing with now, just in a kid version. 

Like, I distinctly remember in third grade—Mrs. Gable's class, she was so sweet but I must have driven her absolutely crazy—she actually had to move my desk right up next to hers. And not because I was being mean or bullying anyone, but because I just could not stay in my seat. I was always popping up to go look out the window, or walking over to see what my friends were drawing, or going to the pencil sharpener for the fifth time. 

And the talking... oh my gosh, the talking. I was constantly blurting out answers before she even finished asking the question. Like, I knew the material, I understood the math or whatever we were doing, but I just couldn't wait my turn. I'd just shout it out. Or I'd rush through my worksheets so fast just to be done, even though I knew how to do the problems, and I'd make all these silly, careless mistakes because I was just flying through it. It's like my brain was always running at a hundred miles an hour and my body was just trying to keep up. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, it's just... I guess it looks different now that I'm an adult trying to function in a professional environment, you know? But the core of it—the not being able to just sit still and wait—that's been there since I was a little kid.
